nameStory: The American octopus gets its straightforward name from being the most common octopus species along the American Atlantic coast. Unlike some octopuses named for exotic locations or dramatic features, this one earned its title simply by being our local representative of these amazing eight-armed creatures.
description: The American octopus is a soft-bodied marine animal with eight flexible arms covered in suction cups. These intelligent creatures can grow to about 2-3 feet across when their arms are spread, though their body (called the mantle) is only about the size of a baseball. They're masters of camouflage, able to instantly change both their color and skin texture to blend with their surroundings. You'll most likely spot one in tide pools or shallow rocky areas along the coast.

idTips.label: Eight arms with suction cups
idTips.description: Count the flexible arms - always exactly eight, each lined with two rows of circular suction cups that feel surprisingly strong if you gently touch them

idTips.label: Color-changing ability
idTips.description: Watch for dramatic color shifts from brown to red to pale yellow, often with spotted or mottled patterns that change in seconds

idTips.label: Soft, squishy texture
idTips.description: The body feels like firm jelly or a water balloon - completely boneless except for a hard beak hidden at the center where the arms meet

idTips.label: Bulging eyes
idTips.description: Large, intelligent-looking eyes that track your movements and seem almost human-like in their alertness

idTips.label: Jet propulsion movement
idTips.description: Moves by shooting water forcefully from a tube-like siphon, creating a sudden backward dart through the water

idTips.label: Rocky hideouts
idTips.description: Look for arms poking out from rock crevices or dens marked by piles of empty shells and crab parts

habitat: American octopuses live in rocky intertidal zones and shallow coastal waters along New England's shoreline, typically in depths from tide pools down to about 100 feet. They prefer areas with plenty of rock crevices, ledges, and caves where they can hide during the day. You're most likely to spot them in tide pools around rocky headlands or while snorkeling in kelp beds and rocky reef areas.

seasonality.spring: Young octopuses become more active as waters warm, often seen in shallow tide pools during low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak viewing season when octopuses are most active and visible in tide pools and shallow waters during early morning or evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Adults are actively feeding and preparing for winter, may be seen hunting crabs and other prey in rocky areas.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold water but still present; look for them in deeper tide pools that don't freeze completely.

funFact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood - two hearts pump blood to the gills while the third pumps blood to the rest of the body, and their blood is blue because it uses copper instead of iron to carry oxygen!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with sea anemones when only the tips of arms are visible, but octopus arms will quickly retreat when touched while anemone tentacles move more slowly. Remember: if it darts away instantly, it's probably an octopus!
contextualKnowledge: **Note: This identification information should be used with caution as detailed information about Octopus americanus specifically is limited, and octopus species identification can be challenging even for experts. Some details may apply more broadly to Atlantic octopuses.**
compareHints: Since no other Octopus species are commonly found in New England waters, compare with squid (which have 10 arms total - 8 regular arms plus 2 longer tentacles) or cuttlefish (rarely seen here, but have a more oval, flattened body). The American octopus is distinguished by having exactly 8 arms of similar length and a more rounded, bag-like body.
